Note that det⁡(I+i​M)det⁡(I−i​M)\frac{{\mathrm{det}}(I+iM)}{{\mathrm{det}}(I-iM)} matches F~F~⋆=g+i​fg−i​f\frac{\tilde{F}}{{\tilde{F}}^{\star}}=\frac{g+i\,f}{g-i\,f} with ff and gg in (128), (130), and (132) when ki=2​Kik_{i}=2K_{i} and δi=2​Δi−ln⁡(2​Ki)\delta_{i}=2\Delta_{i}-\ln(2K_{i}) with Ki>0K_{i}>0.

6 Application to Non-solitonic PDEs

6.1 The Fisher equation with convection

One of the examples discussed in [26] is the Fisher equation with convection term [76, 79],

ut+α​u​ux−ux​x−u⁡(1−u)=0,α≠0,u_{t}+\alpha uu_{x}-u_{xx}-u(1-u)=0,\quad\alpha\neq 0, (136)

where α\alpha is the convection coefficient. This equation can also be viewed as a Burgers equation with quadratic source term. Motivated by a truncated Laurent series, use

u=−2α​(ln⁡f)x=−2α​(fxf)u=-\tfrac{2}{\alpha}(\ln f)_{x}=-\tfrac{2}{\alpha}\left(\frac{f_{x}}{f}\right) (137)

to replace (136) with a homogeneous equation of second degree

f⁡(f3​x+fx−fx​t)+fx​(ft−fx​x+2α​fx)≡f​ℒ​f+𝒩⁡(f,f)=0,f(f_{3x}+f_{x}-f_{xt})+f_{x}(f_{t}-f_{xx}+\tfrac{2}{\alpha}f_{x})\equiv f\,{\cal L}f+{\cal N}(f,f)=0, (138)

where

ℒ​f\displaystyle{\cal L}f =\displaystyle= f3​x+fx−fx​t,\displaystyle f_{3x}+f_{x}-f_{xt}, (139)
𝒩⁡(f,g)\displaystyle{\cal N}(f,g) =\displaystyle= fx​(gt−gx​x+2α​gx).\displaystyle f_{x}(g_{t}-g_{xx}+\tfrac{2}{\alpha}g_{x}). (140)

Seeking a solution of type (28), ℒ​f(1)=ℒ⁡(∑i=1Neθi){\cal L}f^{(1)}={\cal L}(\sum_{i=1}^{N}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{i}}) yields ωi=−(1+ki2).\omega_{i}=-(1+k_{i}^{2}). The second equation in (39) then becomes

ℒf(2)=−∑i=1Nki(1+2αki)e2​θi−∑1≤i<j≤N(ki+kj+4αkikj)eθi+θj.{\cal L}f^{(2)}=-\sum_{i=1}^{N}k_{i}\left(1+\tfrac{2}{\alpha}k_{i}\right)\,{\mathrm{e}}^{2\theta_{i}}-\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\left(k_{i}+k_{j}+\tfrac{4}{\alpha}k_{i}k_{j}\right){\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{i}+\theta_{j}}. (141)

If we were to include the terms e2​θi{\mathrm{e}}^{2\theta_{i}} in f(2)f^{(2)} the perturbation scheme would not terminate. Hence, we are forced to set all wave numbers equal to ki=−α2​(i=1,2,…,N)k_{i}=-\tfrac{\alpha}{2}\;(i=1,2,\ldots,N). Thus, N=1N=1 and only a solitary solution can be obtained. Note that both sums in (141) vanish when ki=−α2k_{i}=-\tfrac{\alpha}{2}. Hence, f(2)=0f^{(2)}=0 and

f⁡(x,t)=1+eθ=1+e−α2​x+14​(4+α2)​t+δ.f(x,t)=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{-\tfrac{\alpha}{2}x+\tfrac{1}{4}(4+\alpha^{2})t+\delta}. (142)

Finally, from (137)

u⁡(x,t)=eθ1+eθ=12​(1−tanh⁡[12​(α2​x−14​(4+α2)​t−δ)]),u(x,t)=\frac{{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}}{1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(1-\tanh\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{\alpha}{2}x-\tfrac{1}{4}(4+\alpha^{2})t-\delta\right)\right]\right), (143)

since k=−α2k=-\tfrac{\alpha}{2}. The graphs of the kink solution (143) in 2D and 3D are similar to those in Fig. 1.

6.2 The Fisher equation

A transformation to homogenize the Fisher equation [18, 80] without convection,

ut−ux​x−u⁡(1−u)=0,u_{t}-u_{xx}-u(1-u)=0, (144)

is remarkably different from (137). Indeed, a truncated Laurent series suggests

u=−6​(ln⁡f)x​x+65​(ln⁡f)t,u=-6(\ln f)_{xx}+\tfrac{6}{5}(\ln f)_{t}, (145)

which yields

f⁡(f4​x+fx​x−65​fx​x​t+15​ft​t−15​ft)−4​fx​f3​x+3​fx​x2−fx2\displaystyle f(f_{4x}+f_{xx}-\tfrac{6}{5}f_{xxt}+\tfrac{1}{5}f_{tt}-\tfrac{1}{5}f_{t})-4f_{x}f_{3x}+3f_{xx}^{2}-f_{x}^{2}
−65​ft​fx​x+125​fx​fx​t+125​ft2≡f​ℒ​f+𝒩⁡(f,f)=0.\displaystyle-\tfrac{6}{5}f_{t}f_{xx}+\tfrac{12}{5}f_{x}f_{xt}+\tfrac{1}{25}f_{t}^{2}\equiv f\,{\cal L}f+{\cal N}(f,f)=0. (146)

Here,

ℒ​f\displaystyle{\cal L}f\! =\displaystyle= f4​x+fx​x−65​fx​x​t+15​ft​t−15​ft,\displaystyle\!f_{4x}+f_{xx}-\tfrac{6}{5}f_{xxt}+\tfrac{1}{5}f_{tt}-\tfrac{1}{5}f_{t}, (147)
𝒩⁡(f,g)\displaystyle{\cal N}(f,g)\! =\displaystyle= −4​fx​g3​x+3​fx​x​gx​x−fx​gx−65​ft​gx​x+125​fx​t​gx+125​ft​gt.\displaystyle\!-4f_{x}g_{3x}+3f_{xx}g_{xx}-f_{x}g_{x}-\tfrac{6}{5}f_{t}g_{xx}+\tfrac{12}{5}f_{xt}g_{x}+\tfrac{1}{25}f_{t}g_{t}. (148)

Solving (39) with f(1)=∑i=1Neθi=∑i=1Neki​x−ωi​t+δif^{(1)}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{i}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}{\mathrm{e}}^{k_{i}\,x-\omega_{i}\,t+\delta_{i}} as a starting point, one gets ωi=−5​ki2\omega_{i}=-5k_{i}^{2} or ωi=−(1+ki2).\omega_{i}=-(1+k_{i}^{2}).

Case 1: For ωi=−5​ki2\omega_{i}=-5k_{i}^{2} the second equation in (39) reads

ℒ​f(2)=∑i=1Nki2​(1−6​ki2)​e2​θi+∑1≤i<j≤Nci​j​eθi+θj,{\cal L}f^{(2)}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}k_{i}^{2}(1-6k_{i}^{2})\,{\mathrm{e}}^{2\theta_{i}}+2\!\!\!\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}c_{ij}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{i}+\theta_{j}}, (149)

where ci​j=ki​kj​[1+2​ki​kj−4​(ki2+kj2)]c_{ij}=k_{i}k_{j}\left[1+2k_{i}k_{j}-4(k_{i}^{2}+k_{j}^{2})\right]. If we put terms e2​θi{\mathrm{e}}^{2\theta_{i}} in f(2)f^{(2)} the perturbation scheme does not terminate. Hence, ki=±16​(i=1,2,…,N)k_{i}=\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\;(i=1,2,\ldots,N) which also makes ci​j=0c_{ij}=0. This leads us to conclude that a multi-soliton solution does not exist and N=1N=1. With k=±16k=\pm\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} we have ω=−56\omega=-\tfrac{5}{6}. Using (145) with f=1+eθf=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta} gives

u⁡(x,t)=e2​θ(1+eθ)2=1(1+e−θ)2=14​(1+tanh⁡θ2)2,u(x,t)=\frac{{\mathrm{e}}^{2\theta}}{(1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta})^{2}}=\frac{1}{(1+e^{-\theta})^{2}}=\tfrac{1}{4}\left(1+\tanh\tfrac{\theta}{2}\right)^{2}, (150)

where each of these forms of the solution appears in the literature (see, e.g., [4]). Explicitly, for k=−16k=-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}},

u⁡(x,t)=14​(1−tanh⁡[12​(16​x−56​t−δ)])2,u(x,t)=\tfrac{1}{4}\left(1-\tanh\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}x-\tfrac{5}{6}t-\delta\right)\right]\right)^{2}, (151)

which is a wave traveling to the right. The graph of this kink solution is the same as in Fig. 1 but with a steeper slope due to the square in (151). For k=16k=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}},

u⁡(x,t)=14​(1+tanh⁡[12​(16​x+56​t+δ)])2,u(x,t)=\tfrac{1}{4}\left(1+\tanh\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}x+\tfrac{5}{6}t+\delta\right)\right]\right)^{2}, (152)

which is a left-traveling wave, a bit steeper than the one shown in Fig. 1 after a vertical flip. Note that (152) does not follow from (143) in the limit for α→0.\alpha\rightarrow 0.

Case 2: For ωi=−(1+ki2)\omega_{i}=-(1+k_{i}^{2}) the second equation in (39) becomes

ℒ​f(2)=−125​(∑i=1N(1+ki2)​(1+6​ki2)​e2​θi+∑1≤i<j≤Nci​j​eθi+θj),{\cal L}f^{(2)}=-\tfrac{1}{25}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}(1+k_{i}^{2})(1+6k_{i}^{2})\,{\mathrm{e}}^{2\theta_{i}}+2\!\!\!\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}c_{ij}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{i}+\theta_{j}}\right), (153)

where ci​j=[1+35​ki​kj+46​ki2​kj2−2​(ki2+kj2)​(7+10​ki​kj)].c_{ij}=\left[1+35k_{i}k_{j}+46k_{i}^{2}k_{j}^{2}-2(k_{i}^{2}+k_{j}^{2})(7+10k_{i}k_{j})\right]. So, for real wave numbers kik_{i} the terms e2​θi{\mathrm{e}}^{2\theta_{i}} do not vanish. No solitary wave solutions or solitons can be obtained in this case.

6.3 The FitzHugh-Nagumo equation with convection

The FHN equation with convection term [58],

ut+α​u​ux−ux​x+u⁡(1−u)​(a−u)=0,u_{t}+\alpha uu_{x}-u_{xx}+u(1-u)(a-u)=0, (154)

where α\alpha denotes the convection coefficient and aa is an arbitrary constant, is also called the Burgers-Huxley equation [87].

A truncated Laurent series suggests two possible transformations, namely,

u=m​(ln⁡f)x=m​(fxf),m>0.u=\sqrt{m}\,(\ln f)_{x}=\sqrt{m}\left(\frac{f_{x}}{f}\right),\quad m>0. (155)

and

u=−2m​(ln⁡f)x=−2m​(fxf),m>0,u=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{m}}\,(\ln f)_{x}=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{m}}\left(\frac{f_{x}}{f}\right),\quad m>0, (156)

where we have replaced α\alpha by m−2m\tfrac{m-2}{\sqrt{m}} in (154) to simplify their forms and the computations below. Using (155), (154) transforms into

f⁡(f3​x−a​fx−fx​t)+fx​(ft−(m+1)​fx​x+m​(1+a)​fx)\displaystyle f(f_{3x}-af_{x}-f_{xt})+f_{x}\left(f_{t}-(m+1)f_{xx}+\sqrt{m}(1+a)f_{x}\right)
≡f​ℒ​f+𝒩⁡(f,f)=0,\displaystyle\equiv f\,{\cal L}f+{\cal N}(f,f)=0, (157)

where

ℒ​f\displaystyle{\cal L}f =\displaystyle= f3​x−a​fx−fx​t,\displaystyle f_{3x}-af_{x}-f_{xt}, (158)
𝒩⁡(f,g)\displaystyle{\cal N}(f,g) =\displaystyle= fx​(gt−(m+1)​gx​x+m​(1+a)​gx).\displaystyle f_{x}\left(g_{t}-(m+1)g_{xx}+\sqrt{m}(1+a)g_{x}\right). (159)

To compute a single solitary wave solution we take f=1+eθf=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}. Then, ℒ​eθ=0{\cal L}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}=0 yields ω=a−k2\omega=a-k^{2}. Next, 𝒩⁡(eθ,eθ)=0{\cal N}({\mathrm{e}}^{\theta},{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta})=0 determines k=1mk=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}} or k=am.k=\tfrac{a}{\sqrt{m}}. Thus, ω=a​m−1m\omega=\tfrac{am-1}{m} or ω=a⁡(m−a)m,\omega=\tfrac{a(m-a)}{m}, respectively. Returning to uu, we obtain the solitary wave solutions

u⁡(x,t)=12​(1+tanh⁡[12​(1m​x−(a​m−1)m​t+δ)])u(x,t)=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(1+\tanh\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}x-\frac{(am-1)}{m}t+\delta\right)\right]\right) (160)

and

u⁡(x,t)=12​a​(1+tanh⁡[12​(am​x−a⁡(m−a)m​t+δ)]).u(x,t)=\tfrac{1}{2}a\left(1+\tanh\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{m}}x-\frac{a(m-a)}{m}t+\delta\right)\right]\right). (161)

Although it is impossible to find a two-soliton solution, a so-called bi-soliton solution can be computed which describes coalescent wave fronts. Indeed, taking f=1+eθ1+eθ2,f=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}}, with ωi=a−ki2​(i=1,2)\omega_{i}=a-k_{i}^{2}\;(i=1,2), after some computations one gets

u⁡(x,t)=eθ1+a​eθ21+eθ1+eθ2,u(x,t)=\frac{{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+a\,{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}}}{1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}}}, (162)

where

θ1=1m​x−(a​m−1m)​t+δ1,θ2=am​x−(a⁡(m−a)m)​t+δ2.\theta_{1}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}x-\left(\tfrac{am-1}{m}\right)t+\delta_{1},\;\;\theta_{2}=\tfrac{a}{\sqrt{m}}x-\left(\tfrac{a(m-a)}{m}\right)t+\delta_{2}. (163)

Since α=m−2m\alpha=\tfrac{m-2}{\sqrt{m}}, possible1717 17 For any positive value of mm, the pair (α,m)(\alpha,m) must still satisfy α=m−2m\alpha=\tfrac{m-2}{\sqrt{m}}. values for mm are

m=12​(4+α2±α​8+α2),m>0.m=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(4+\alpha^{2}\pm\alpha\sqrt{8+\alpha^{2}}\right),\quad m>0. (164)

This solution can be found in [30] and [58] where it was obtained with a different method.

Skipping the details, with (156) one obtains the following solutions

u⁡(x,t)=12​(1−tanh⁡[12​(m2​x+(4​a−m)4​t−δ)])u(x,t)=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(1-\tanh\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{m}}{2}x+\frac{(4a-m)}{4}t-\delta\right)\right]\right) (165)

and

u⁡(x,t)=12​a​(1−tanh⁡[12​(a​m2​x+a⁡(4−a​m)4​t−δ)]),u(x,t)=\tfrac{1}{2}a\left(1-\tanh\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{a\sqrt{m}}{2}x+\frac{a(4-am)}{4}t-\delta\right)\right]\right), (166)

with mm given in (164). The bi-soliton solution corresponding to (156) is (162) with

θ1=−m2​x−(4​a−m4)​t+δ1,θ2=−a​m2​x−(a⁡(4−a​m)4)​t+δ2.\theta_{1}=-\tfrac{\sqrt{m}}{2}x-\left(\tfrac{4a-m}{4}\right)t+\delta_{1},\;\;\theta_{2}=-\tfrac{a\sqrt{m}}{2}x-\left(\tfrac{a(4-am)}{4}\right)t+\delta_{2}. (167)

Solution (162) with either (163) or (167) describes the coalescence of two wave fronts pictured in Fig. 14.

Finally, for m=2m=2 (i.e., α=0\alpha=0), one gets a solitary wave solution of the FHN equation without convection [5].

6.4 A Burgers equation with a cubic source term

Consider the Burgers equation with a polynomial source term of third degree,

ut+α​u​ux−ux​x=3​u​(2−u)​(u+1),u_{t}+\alpha uu_{x}-u_{xx}=3u(2-u)(u+1), (168)

which is of the kind treated in (99, Eq. (26)). Eq. (168) can also be viewed as an equation of FitzHugh-Naguma-type with convection term1818 18 Except that u−1u-1 is now replaced by u+1u+1.. Such equations are known to have coalescent wave fronts [27, 58]. Based on a truncated Laurent series, there are potentially two homogenizing transformations:

u=m​(ln⁡f)x=m​(fxf),m>0.u=\sqrt{m}\,(\ln f)_{x}=\sqrt{m}\left(\frac{f_{x}}{f}\right),\quad m>0. (169)

and

u=−23​m​(ln⁡f)x=−23​m​(fxf),m>0,u=-\frac{2}{3\sqrt{m}}\,(\ln f)_{x}=-\frac{2}{3\sqrt{m}}\left(\frac{f_{x}}{f}\right),\quad m>0, (170)

where we used α=3​m−2m\alpha=\tfrac{3m-2}{\sqrt{m}} in (168) to simplify their forms. Starting with (169), substitution into (168) yields

f⁡(6​fx−fx​t+f3​x)+fx​(ft+3​m​fx−(1+3​m)​fx​x)\displaystyle f\left(6f_{x}-f_{xt}+f_{3x}\right)+f_{x}\left(f_{t}+3\sqrt{m}f_{x}-\left(1+3m\right)f_{xx}\right) (171)
≡f​ℒ​f+𝒩⁡(f,f)=0.\displaystyle\equiv f\,{\cal L}f+{\cal N}(f,f)=0. (172)

Here, ℒ{\cal L} and 𝒩{\cal N} are defined by

ℒ​f\displaystyle{\cal L}f =\displaystyle= 6​fx−fx​t+f3​x,\displaystyle 6f_{x}-f_{xt}+f_{3x}, (173)
𝒩⁡(f,g)\displaystyle{\cal N}(f,g) =\displaystyle= fx​(gt+3​m​gx−(1+3​m)​gx​x).\displaystyle f_{x}\left(g_{t}+3\sqrt{m}g_{x}-\left(1+3m\right)g_{xx}\right). (174)

For the single solitary wave solution, ℒ​eθ=0{\cal L}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}=0 yields ω=−(k2+6)\omega=-(k^{2}+6). Next, 𝒩⁡(eθ,eθ)=0{\cal N}({\mathrm{e}}^{\theta},{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta})=0 determines k=−1mk=-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}} or k=2m.k=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{m}}. Thus, ω=−6​m+1m\omega=-\tfrac{6m+1}{m} or ω=−2​(3​m+2)m,\omega=-\tfrac{2(3m+2)}{m}, respectively. So, with f=1+eθf=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta} we obtain the solitary wave solutions

u⁡(x,t)=−12​(1−tanh⁡[12​m​x−(6​m+1)2​m​t−δ2])u(x,t)=-\tfrac{1}{2}\left(1-\tanh\left[\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{m}}x-\frac{(6m+1)}{2m}t-\frac{\delta}{2}\right]\right) (175)

and

u⁡(x,t)=1+tanh⁡[1m​x+(3​m+2)m​t+δ2],u(x,t)=1+\tanh\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}x+\frac{(3m+2)}{m}t+\frac{\delta}{2}\right], (176)

where, with regard to α=3​m−2m\alpha=\tfrac{3m-2}{\sqrt{m}}, possible values1919 19 For any positive value of mm, the pair (α,m)(\alpha,m) must still satisfy α=3​m−2m\alpha=\tfrac{3m-2}{\sqrt{m}}. for mm are

m=118​(12+α2±α​24+α2),m>0.m=\tfrac{1}{18}\left(12+\alpha^{2}\pm\alpha\sqrt{24+\alpha^{2}}\right),\quad m>0. (177)

As with the FHN equation with convection term, no two-soliton solution exists but a bi-soliton solution can be found which describes coalescent wave fronts. Indeed, taking f=1+eθ1+eθ2f=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}} where ωi=−(ki2+6)​(i=1,2)\omega_{i}=-(k_{i}^{2}+6)\;(i=1,2) one gets

u⁡(x,t)\displaystyle u(x,t) =\displaystyle= m​(k1​eθ1+k2​eθ2)1+eθ1+eθ2\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{m}(k_{1}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+k_{2}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}})}{1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}}} (178)
=\displaystyle= 2​e2m​x+2​(3​m+2)m​t+δ1−e−1m​x+(6​m+1)m​t+δ21+e2m​x+2​(3​m+2)m​t+δ1+e−1m​x+(6​m+1)m​t+δ2,\displaystyle\frac{2\,{\mathrm{e}}^{\frac{2}{\sqrt{m}}x+\frac{2(3m+2)}{m}t+\delta_{1}}-{\mathrm{e}}^{-\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}x+\frac{(6m+1)}{m}t+\delta_{2}}}{1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\frac{2}{\sqrt{m}}x+\frac{2(3m+2)}{m}t+\delta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{-\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}x+\frac{(6m+1)}{m}t+\delta_{2}}},

because k1=2mk_{1}=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{m}} and k2=−1mk_{2}=-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}} with mm in (177). For m=1m=1, a solution of (168) with α=1\alpha=1 then reads

u⁡(x,t)=2​e2​x+10​t+δ1−e−x+7​t+δ21+e2​x+10​t+δ1+e−x+7​t+δ2.u(x,t)=\frac{2{\mathrm{e}}^{2x+10t+\delta_{1}}-{\mathrm{e}}^{-x+7t+\delta_{2}}}{1+{\mathrm{e}}^{2x+10t+\delta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{-x+7t+\delta_{2}}}. (179)

The solution procedure using (170) is similar and leads to

u⁡(x,t)=−12​(1+tanh⁡[3​m4​x+3​(3​m+8)8​t+δ2])u(x,t)=-\tfrac{1}{2}\left(1+\tanh\left[\tfrac{3\sqrt{m}}{4}x+\frac{3(3m+8)}{8}t+\frac{\delta}{2}\right]\right) (180)

and

u⁡(x,t)=1−tanh⁡[3​m2​x−3​(3​m+2)2​t−δ2],u(x,t)=1-\tanh\left[\frac{3\sqrt{m}}{2}x-\frac{3(3m+2)}{2}t-\frac{\delta}{2}\right], (181)

with mm given in (177). The bi-soliton solution corresponding to (170) reads

u⁡(x,t)\displaystyle u(x,t) =\displaystyle= −23​m​(k1​eθ1+k2​eθ2)(1+eθ1+eθ2)\displaystyle-\frac{2}{3\sqrt{m}}\frac{(k_{1}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+k_{2}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}})}{(1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}})} (182)
=\displaystyle= −e3​m2​x+3​(3​m+8)4​t+δ1−2​e−3​m​x+3​(3​m+2)​t+δ21+e3​m2​x+3​(3​m+8)4​t+δ1+e−3​m​x+3​(3​m+2)​t+δ2,\displaystyle-\frac{{\mathrm{e}}^{\frac{3\sqrt{m}}{2}x+\frac{3(3m+8)}{4}t+\delta_{1}}-2\,{\mathrm{e}}^{-3\sqrt{m}x+3(3m+2)t+\delta_{2}}}{1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\frac{3\sqrt{m}}{2}x+\frac{3(3m+8)}{4}t+\delta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{-3\sqrt{m}x+3(3m+2)t+\delta_{2}}},

because k1=3​m2k_{1}=\frac{3\sqrt{m}}{2} and k2=−3​mk_{2}=-3\sqrt{m} with mm in (177). For m=1m=1, a bi-soliton solution of (168) with α=1\alpha=1 then becomes

u⁡(x,t)=−e32​x+334​t+δ1−2​e−3​x+15​t+δ21+e32​x+334​t+δ1+e−3​x+15​t+δ2.u(x,t)=-\frac{{\mathrm{e}}^{\frac{3}{2}x+\frac{33}{4}t+\delta_{1}}-2{\mathrm{e}}^{-3x+15t+\delta_{2}}}{1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\frac{3}{2}x+\frac{33}{4}t+\delta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{-3x+15t+\delta_{2}}}. (183)

Solutions (179) and (183), describing two coalescent wave fronts, are shown in Fig. 15.

Returning to α\alpha via (177) also allows one to consider the case α=0\alpha=0 (i.e., m=23m=\tfrac{2}{3}), leading to solutions of (168) with a cubic source but without convection.

6.5 A wave equation with cubic source term

Consider the wave equation,

18​ut​t+ut+u​ux−18​ux​x=u⁡(u−1)​(u+2),\tfrac{1}{8}u_{tt}+u_{t}+uu_{x}-\tfrac{1}{8}u_{xx}=u(u-1)(u+2), (184)

which is a special case of an equation investigated in (99, Eq. (2)). The Laurent series solution suggests the transformation

u=12​κ​[(ln⁡f)t−κ​(ln⁡f)x]=12​κ​(ft−κ​fxf),u=\tfrac{1}{2}\kappa\left[(\ln f)_{t}-\kappa(\ln f)_{x}\right]=\tfrac{1}{2}\kappa\left(\frac{f_{t}-\kappa f_{x}}{f}\right), (185)

with κ=±1.\kappa=\pm 1. We first consider the case where κ=1\kappa=1. Using

u=12​(ft−fxf),u=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{f_{t}-f_{x}}{f}\right), (186)

allows one to replace (184) by

f⁡(16​ft+8​ft​t+f3​t−16​fx−8​fx​t−fx​t​t−fx​x​t+f3​x)\displaystyle f\left(16f_{t}+8f_{tt}+f_{3t}-16f_{x}-8f_{xt}-f_{xtt}-f_{xxt}+f_{3x}\right)
−(3​ft−fx)​(4​ft+ft​t−4​fx−2​fx​t+fx​x)\displaystyle-\left(3f_{t}-f_{x}\right)\left(4f_{t}+f_{tt}-4f_{x}-2f_{xt}+f_{xx}\right)
≡f​ℒ​f+𝒩⁡(f,f)=0,\displaystyle\equiv f\,{\cal L}f+{\cal N}(f,f)=0, (187)

with

ℒ​f\displaystyle{\cal L}f =\displaystyle= 16​ft+8​ft​t+f3​t−16​fx−8​fx​t−fx​t​t−fx​x​t+f3​x,\displaystyle 16f_{t}+8f_{tt}+f_{3t}-16f_{x}-8f_{xt}-f_{xtt}-f_{xxt}+f_{3x}, (188)
𝒩⁡(f,g)\displaystyle{\cal N}(f,g) =\displaystyle= −(3​ft−fx)​(4​gt+gt​t−4​gx−2​gx​t+gx​x).\displaystyle-\left(3f_{t}-f_{x}\right)\left(4g_{t}+g_{tt}-4g_{x}-2g_{xt}+g_{xx}\right). (189)

Then, ℒ​eθ=0{\cal L}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}=0 yields ω=−k,ω=4−k,\omega=-k,\,\omega=4-k, or ω=4+k.\omega=4+k. With f=1+eθ,f=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}, one readily obtains

u⁡(x,t)=−12​(ω+k)​(eθ1+eθ)=−14​(ω+k)​(1+tanh⁡θ2).u(x,t)=-\tfrac{1}{2}(\omega+k)\left(\frac{{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}}{1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}}\right)=-\tfrac{1}{4}(\omega+k)\left(1+\tanh\tfrac{\theta}{2}\right). (190)

Obviously, the choice ω=−k\omega=-k must be rejected. For ω=4−k,\omega=4-k, one finds that 𝒩⁡(eθ,eθ)≡0{\cal N}({\mathrm{e}}^{\theta},{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta})\equiv 0 and

u⁡(x,t)=−(1+tanh⁡[12​(k​x−(4−k)​t+δ)])u(x,t)=-\left(1+\tanh\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\left(kx-(4-k)t+\delta\right)\right]\right) (191)

with arbitrary kk and δ\delta. For ω=4+k\omega=4+k, 𝒩⁡(eθ,eθ)=0{\cal N}({\mathrm{e}}^{\theta},{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta})=0 determines k=−2k=-2 or k=−3k=-3 resulting in ω=2\omega=2 or ω=1,\omega=1, respectively. The case k=−2k=-2 (i.e., ω=2\omega=2) is rejected for it leads to u⁡(x,t)≡0.u(x,t)\equiv 0. For k=−3k=-3 (i.e., ω=1\omega=1) one gets

u⁡(x,t)=12​(1−tanh⁡[12​(3​x+t−δ)]),u(x,t)=\tfrac{1}{2}\Big(1-\tanh\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\left(3x+t-\delta\right)\right]\Big), (192)

which is different from (191) when k=−3k=-3.

Attempting to find a solution of type (28), ℒ​f(1)=ℒ⁡(∑i=1Neθi){\cal L}f^{(1)}={\cal L}(\sum_{i=1}^{N}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{i}}) determines ωi=−ki,4−ki,\omega_{i}=-k_{i},4-k_{i}, or 4+ki.4+k_{i}. As with the solitary wave solution, to avoid trivial solutions we continue with ωi=4−ki\omega_{i}=4-k_{i} and ωi=4+ki\omega_{i}=4+k_{i}.

Here again, it is impossible to find a two-soliton solution but a bi-soliton solution can be computed. Indeed, taking f=1+eθ1+eθ2+a12​eθ1+θ2,f=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}}+a_{12}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}}, leads to a12=0.a_{12}=0. Then, for ωi=4−ki​(i=1,2)\omega_{i}=4-k_{i}\;(i=1,2), after some computation one gets

u​(x,t)=−2​(eθ1+eθ21+eθ1+eθ2),u(x,t)=-2\left(\frac{{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}}}{1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}}}\right), (193)

where θ1=k1​x−(4−k1)​t+δ1\theta_{1}=k_{1}x-(4-k_{1})t+\delta_{1} and θ2=k2​x−(4−k2)​t+δ2\theta_{2}=k_{2}x-(4-k_{2})t+\delta_{2}. Solution (193) agrees with the result in (99, Eq. (37)). As shown in Fig. 16, (193) describes two coalescent wave fronts. For ωi=4+ki,\omega_{i}=4+k_{i}, after some computations one gets k1=−2,k2=−3k_{1}=-2,k_{2}=-3, and a12=1a_{12}=1, resulting in (192) with δ\delta replaced by δ2\delta_{2}.

The computations for κ=−1\kappa=-1 in (185) are similar but only lead to

u⁡(x,t)=12​(1+tanh⁡[12​(x−3​t+δ)])u(x,t)=\tfrac{1}{2}\Big(1+\tanh\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\left(x-3t+\delta\right)\right]\Big) (194)

which does not follow from (191) when k=1k=1.

6.6 A combined KdV-Burgers equation

A combined KdV-Burgers equation [98],

ut+6​u​ux+u3​x−5​β​ux​x=0,u_{t}+6uu_{x}+u_{3x}-5\beta u_{xx}=0, (195)

where β>0\beta>0, is used in models where both dispersive and dissipative effects are relevant. A Laurent series of the solution of (195) suggests the transformation

u=2​(ln⁡f)x​x−2​β​(ln⁡f)x,u=2(\ln f)_{xx}-2\beta(\ln f)_{x}, (196)

which we substitute into the integrated KdV-Burgers equation,

∂t(∫xu​𝑑x)+3​u2+ux​x−5​β​ux=0\partial_{t}\left(\int^{x}u\,dx\right)+3u^{2}+u_{xx}-5\beta u_{x}=0 (197)

to get

f⁡(fx​t−β​ft+5​β2​fx​x−6​β​f3​x+f4​x)\displaystyle f(f_{xt}-\beta f_{t}+5\beta^{2}f_{xx}-6\beta f_{3x}+f_{4x})
−fx​ft+β2​fx2+6​β​fx​fx​x+3​fx​x2−4​fx​f3​x=0.\displaystyle-f_{x}f_{t}+\beta^{2}f_{x}^{2}+6\beta f_{x}f_{xx}+3f_{xx}^{2}-4f_{x}f_{3x}=0. (198)

This homogeneous equation is of the form f​ℒ​f+𝒩⁡(f,f)=0.f\,{\cal L}f+{\cal N}(f,f)=0. Therefore, we can proceed as in the KdV case and solve (39) step-by-step with

ℒ​f\displaystyle{\cal L}f =\displaystyle= fx​t−β​ft+5​β2​fx​x−6​β​f3​x+f4​x,\displaystyle f_{xt}-\beta f_{t}+5\beta^{2}f_{xx}-6\beta f_{3x}+f_{4x}, (199)
𝒩⁡(f,g)\displaystyle{\cal N}(f,g) =\displaystyle= −fx​gt+β2​fx​gx+6​β​fx​gx​x+3​fx​x​gx​x−4​fx​g3​x.\displaystyle-f_{x}g_{t}+\beta^{2}f_{x}g_{x}+6\beta f_{x}g_{xx}+3f_{xx}g_{xx}-4f_{x}g_{3x}. (200)

We summarize the results. First, ℒ​eθ=ℒ​ek​x−ω​t+δ=0{\cal L}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}={\cal L}{\mathrm{e}}^{kx-\omega t+\delta}=0 yields (β−k)​(ω−k3+5​β​k2)=0(\beta-k)(\omega-k^{3}+5\beta k^{2})=0. Thus, two cases have to be considered.

Case 1: When ω=k2​(k−5​β)\omega=k^{2}(k-5\beta) and k≠βk\neq\beta, 𝒩⁡(eθ,eθ)=0{\cal N}({\mathrm{e}}^{\theta},{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta})=0 determines k=−βk=-\beta. So, ω=−6​β3\omega=-6\beta^{3}. Inserting f=1+eθf=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta} into (196) yields

u⁡(x,t)=2​β2​(eθ​(2+eθ)(1+eθ)2)=12​β2​(3−tanh⁡θ2)​(1+tanh⁡θ2),u(x,t)=2\beta^{2}\left(\frac{{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}(2+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta})}{(1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta})^{2}}\right)=\tfrac{1}{2}\beta^{2}\left(3-\tanh\tfrac{\theta}{2}\right)\left(1+\tanh\tfrac{\theta}{2}\right), (201)

with θ=−β​x+6​β3​t+δ\theta=-\beta x+6\beta^{3}t+\delta.

Case 2: When k=βk=\beta, 𝒩⁡(eθ,eθ)=0{\cal N}({\mathrm{e}}^{\theta},{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta})=0 determines ω=−6​β3\omega=-6\beta^{3}, yielding

u⁡(x,t)=−2​β2​(e2​θ(1+eθ)2)=−12​β2​(1+tanh⁡θ2)2,u(x,t)=-2\beta^{2}\left(\frac{{\mathrm{e}}^{2\theta}}{(1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta})^{2}}\right)=-\tfrac{1}{2}\beta^{2}\left(1+\tanh\tfrac{\theta}{2}\right)^{2}, (202)

with θ=β​x+6​β3​t+δ\theta=\beta x+6\beta^{3}t+\delta. Solutions (201) and (202) are shown in Fig. 17 for β=2\beta=2 and δ=0\delta=0.

An attempt to find a multi-soliton or bi-soliton solutions based on (28) failed. Assuming ki≠βk_{i}\neq\beta (discussed in Case 2) and working with (28), ℒ​f(1)=ℒ⁡(∑i=1Neθi){\cal L}f^{(1)}={\cal L}(\sum_{i=1}^{N}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{i}}) determines ωi=ki2​(ki−5​β)\omega_{i}=k_{i}^{2}(k_{i}-5\beta). The second equation in (39) then becomes

ℒf(2)=−β∑i=1Nki2(ki+β)e2​θi−∑1≤i<j≤Nci​jeθi+θj,{\cal L}f^{(2)}=-\beta\sum_{i=1}^{N}k_{i}^{2}(k_{i}+\beta)\,{\mathrm{e}}^{2\theta_{i}}-\!\!\!\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}c_{ij}\,{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{i}+\theta_{j}}, (203)

where ci​j=ki​kj​[2​β2+β⁡(ki+kj)+6​ki​kj−3​(ki2+kj2)].c_{ij}=k_{i}k_{j}\left[2\beta^{2}+\beta(k_{i}+k_{j})+6k_{i}k_{j}-3(k_{i}^{2}+k_{j}^{2})\right]. Putting terms e2​θi{\mathrm{e}}^{2\theta_{i}} in f(2)f^{(2)} prevents the perturbation scheme from terminating. Hence, ki=−β⁡(i=1,2,…,N)k_{i}=-\beta\;(i=1,2,\ldots,N) which also makes ci​j=0c_{ij}=0. But if the wave numbers have to be equal then N=1N=1 and that brings us back to Case 1 and (201).

6.7 An equation due to Calogero

For the equation

ut−3​(3​u​ux2+u4​ux+u2​ux​x)−u3​x=0u_{t}-3(3uu_{x}^{2}+u^{4}u_{x}+u^{2}u_{xx})-u_{3x}=0 (204)

due to Calogero [8], the Laurent series (7) has α=−12\alpha=-\tfrac{1}{2}. Therefore, to apply the simplified Hirota method we first change the dependent variable. Setting u=vu=\sqrt{v} with v>0v>0 gives

4​v2​vt−3​vx3−12​v2​vx2−12​v4​vx+6​v​vx​vx​x−12​v3​vx​x−4​v2​v3​x=0,4v^{2}v_{t}-3v_{x}^{3}-12v^{2}v_{x}^{2}-12v^{4}v_{x}+6vv_{x}v_{xx}-12v^{3}v_{xx}-4v^{2}v_{3x}=0, (205)

which looks more complicated than (204) but has a truncated Laurent series with α=−1\alpha=-1. Then, with the transformation

v=12​(ln⁡f)x=12​(fxf)v=\tfrac{1}{2}(\ln f)_{x}=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{f_{x}}{f}\right) (206)

(205) can be replaced by an equation of fourth degree,

f⁡(4​fx2​fx​t−3​fx​x3+6​fx​fx​x​f3​x−4​fx2​f4​x)−fx2​(4​fx​ft+3​fx​x2−4​fx​f3​x)\displaystyle f(4f_{x}^{2}f_{xt}-3f_{xx}^{3}+6f_{x}f_{xx}f_{3x}-4f_{x}^{2}f_{4x})-f_{x}^{2}(4f_{x}f_{t}+3f_{xx}^{2}-4f_{x}f_{3x})
≡f​𝒩1​(f,f,f)+𝒩2​(f,f,f,f)=0,\displaystyle\equiv f\,{\cal N}_{1}(f,f,f)+{\cal N}_{2}(f,f,f,f)=0, (207)

with

𝒩1​(f,g,h)\displaystyle{\cal N}_{1}(f,g,h) =\displaystyle= 4​fx​gx​hx​t−3​fx​x​gx​x​hx​x+6​fx​gx​x​h3​x−4​fx​gx​h4​x,\displaystyle 4f_{x}g_{x}h_{xt}-3f_{xx}g_{xx}h_{xx}+6f_{x}g_{xx}h_{3x}-4f_{x}g_{x}h_{4x}, (208)
𝒩2​(f,g,h,j)\displaystyle{\cal N}_{2}(f,g,h,j) =\displaystyle= −fx​gx​(4​hx​jt+3​hx​x​jx​x−4​hx​j3​x).\displaystyle-f_{x}g_{x}(4h_{x}j_{t}+3h_{xx}j_{xx}-4h_{x}j_{3x}). (209)

If one seeks a solution to (207) of type (28), then 𝒩1​(eθ,eθ,eθ){\cal N}_{1}({\mathrm{e}}^{\theta},{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta},{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}) with θ=k​x−ω​t+δ\theta=kx-\omega t+\delta yields ω=−14​k3\omega=-\tfrac{1}{4}k^{3}. Fortuitously, if the dispersion law holds then 𝒩2​(eθ,eθ,eθ,eθ)=0{\cal N}_{2}({\mathrm{e}}^{\theta},{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta},{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta},{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta})=0 and, therefore, f=1+eθf=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta} solves (207). Using (206) and u=vu=\sqrt{v}, after some algebra one gets

u=12​k​1+tanh⁡[18​(4​k​x+k3​t+4​δ)],u=\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{k}\,\sqrt{1+\tanh\left[\tfrac{1}{8}\left(4kx+k^{3}t+4\delta\right)\right]}, (210)

where k>0k>0. This solution was computed in [30] with a different method. It is graphed in Fig. 18 for k=4k=4 and δ=0\delta=0.

If one tries to find a multi-soliton solution with f(1)=∑i=1Neθif^{(1)}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{i}} with θi=ki​x+14​ki3​t+δi,\theta_{i}=k_{i}x+\tfrac{1}{4}k_{i}^{3}t+\delta_{i}, then 𝒩1​(f(1),f(1),f(1)){\cal N}_{1}(f^{(1)},f^{(1)},f^{(1)}) only vanishes if the wave numbers are equal.

7 An Equation with Two but not Three Solitons

Equations that have two-soliton but not three-soliton solutions have been discovered. The best known example is the sine-Gordon equation in two space variables which already appears in early work by Hirota [44] and was later studied in greater generality in [59]. Another example is a (3+1)(3+1)-dimensional eight-order equation due to Kac-Wakimoto [90, 105].

With respect to equations in (1+1)(1+1) dimensions, Hietarinta (see [36, 37] and references therein) did an extensive search of bilinear forms for which the necessary condition to have a three-soliton solution is violated. Although the appropriate bilinear forms are given explicitly, the equations in the original field variable uu are not always available in his papers. Reversing the process, i.e., finding the nonlinear PDE (or a system thereof) that leads to a (known) bilinear form is not straightforward. Consult, e.g., [36, 37, 40, 70] for strategies and explicit examples.

Taking a different example, we study the soliton solutions of a polynomial equation in (1+1)(1+1) dimensions,

ut+15784​u3​ux+1528​u​ux​ux​x+1556​u2​u3​x+52​ux​x​u3​x+ux​u4​x+u​u5​x+u7​x=0,u_{t}+\tfrac{15}{784}u^{3}u_{x}+\tfrac{15}{28}uu_{x}u_{xx}+\tfrac{15}{56}u^{2}u_{3x}+\tfrac{5}{2}u_{xx}u_{3x}+u_{x}u_{4x}+uu_{5x}+u_{7x}=0, (211)

which appears in (51, Eq. (19) for K=56K=56). The authors claim that this equation has at most a two-soliton solution. However, they do not give the constraint on the wave numbers kik_{i} that prevents the existence of, e.g., a three-soliton solution. We therefore investigate (211) in more detail.

Based on a truncated Laurent series, we substitute

u=56​(ln⁡f)x​x=56​(f​fx​x−fx2f2)u=56\,(\ln f)_{xx}=56\left(\frac{ff_{xx}-{f_{x}}^{2}}{f^{2}}\right) (212)

into the integrated form of (211),

∂t(∫xu​𝑑x)+153136​u4+1556​u2​ux​x+54​ux​x2+u​u4​x+u6​x=0,\partial_{t}\left(\int^{x}u\,dx\right)+\tfrac{15}{3136}u^{4}+\tfrac{15}{56}u^{2}u_{xx}+\tfrac{5}{4}u_{xx}^{2}+uu_{4x}+u_{6x}=0, (213)

yielding

f⁡(fx​t+f8​x)−fx​ft+35​f4​x2−56​f3​x​f5​x+28​fx​x​f6​x−8​fx​f7​x=0,f\left(f_{xt}+f_{8x}\right)-f_{x}f_{t}+35{f_{4x}}^{2}-56f_{3x}f_{5x}+28f_{xx}f_{6x}-8f_{x}f_{7x}=0, (214)

which is of the form f​ℒ​f+𝒩⁡(f,f)=0f{\cal L}f+{\cal N}(f,f)=0 with

ℒ​f\displaystyle{\cal L}f =\displaystyle= fx​t+f8​x,\displaystyle f_{xt}+f_{8x}, (215)
𝒩⁡(f,g)\displaystyle{\cal N}(f,g) =\displaystyle= −fx​gt+35​f4​x​g4​x−56​f3​x​g5​x+28​fx​x​g6​x−8​fx​g7​x.\displaystyle-f_{x}g_{t}+35f_{4x}g_{4x}-56f_{3x}g_{5x}+28f_{xx}g_{6x}-8f_{x}g_{7x}. (216)

As usual, ℒ​eθ=0{\cal L}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}=0 yields the dispersion relation ω=k7.\omega=k^{7}. So, with f=1+eθf=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta} we obtain the solitary wave solution

u⁡(x,t)=14​k2​sech2​[12​(k​x−k7​t+δ)].u(x,t)=14k^{2}{\mathrm{sech}}^{2}\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\left(kx-k^{7}t+\delta\right)\right]. (217)

Seeking a solution of the form (28), as before ℒ​f(1)=ℒ⁡(∑i=1Neθi)=0{\cal L}f^{(1)}={\cal L}(\sum_{i=1}^{N}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{i}})=0 with θi=ki​x−ωi​t+δi\theta_{i}=k_{i}x-\omega_{i}t+\delta_{i} yields ωi=ki7\omega_{i}={k_{i}}^{7}.

For the two-soliton solution, taking f=1+eθ1+eθ2+a12​eθ1+θ2f=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}}+a_{12}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}}, after some computations one gets

a12=((k1−k2)​(k12−k1​k2+k22)(k1+k2)​(k12+k1​k2+k22))2a_{12}=\left(\frac{(k_{1}-k_{2})\left({k_{1}}^{2}-k_{1}k_{2}+{k_{2}}^{2}\right)}{(k_{1}+k_{2})\left({k_{1}}^{2}+k_{1}k_{2}+{k_{2}}^{2}\right)}\right)^{2} (218)

and, then from (212),

u⁡(x,t)\displaystyle u(x,t) =\displaystyle= 56​(k12​eθ1+k22​eθ2+a12​eθ1+θ2​(k1+k2)21+eθ1+eθ2+a12​eθ1+θ2CLOSE\displaystyle 56\left(\frac{{k_{1}}^{2}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+{k_{2}}^{2}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}}+a_{12}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}}(k_{1}+k_{2})^{2}}{1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}}+a_{12}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}}}\right. (219)
OPEN−(k1​eθ1+k2​eθ2+a12​eθ1+θ2​(k1+k2))2(1+eθ1+eθ2+a12​eθ1+θ2)2)\displaystyle\left.-\frac{\left(k_{1}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+k_{2}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}}+a_{12}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}}(k_{1}+k_{2})\right)^{2}}{(1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}}+a_{12}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}})^{2}}\right)

with θi=ki​x−ki7​t+δi\theta_{i}=k_{i}x-{k_{i}}^{7}t+\delta_{i}.

The collision of two solitons for equation (211) is shown in Figs. 19 and 20 for k1=1,k2=2,k_{1}=1,\,k_{2}=2, and δ1=δ2=0\delta_{1}=\delta_{2}=0.

The existence of a two-soliton solution comes as no surprise because (214) can be written in bilinear form as

(Dx​Dt+Dx8)​(f⋅f)=0,\left(D_{x}D_{t}+D_{x}^{8}\right)(f\mathbf{\cdot}f)=0, (220)

which satisfies the conditions2020 20 For a derivation of such conditions see, e.g., [74]. for the existence of a two-soliton solution (see, for example, (34, Eq. (22)) and (46, Eq. (5.47))).

In an attempt to find a three-soliton solution, one would take

f=1+eθ1+eθ2+eθ3+a12​eθ1+θ2+a13​eθ1+θ3+a23​eθ2+θ3+b123​eθ1+θ2+θ3f=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{3}}+a_{12}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}}+a_{13}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}+\theta_{3}}+a_{23}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}+\theta_{3}}+b_{123}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}+\theta_{3}} (221)

with

ai​j=((ki−kj)​(ki2−ki​kj+kj2)(ki+kj)​(ki2+ki​kj+kj2))2a_{ij}=\left(\frac{(k_{i}-k_{j})\left({k_{i}}^{2}-k_{i}k_{j}+{k_{j}}^{2}\right)}{(k_{i}+k_{j})\left({k_{i}}^{2}+k_{i}k_{j}+{k_{j}}^{2}\right)}\right)^{2} (222)

and b123=a12​a13​a23b_{123}=a_{12}a_{13}a_{23} and substitute it into (214). A lengthy computation shows that the equation is only satisfied if the wave numbers are equal or zero. Actually, this agrees with Hietarinta’s earlier studies of equations that have a bilinear form. Indeed, for an NN-soliton solution to exist, the condition [46, 74]

S[P,n]=∑σ=±1P(∑i=1nσiki,−∑i=1nσiωi)∏i<j(n)P(σiki−σjkj,−σiωi+σjωj)σiσj=0S[P,n]\!=\!\sum_{\sigma=\pm 1}\!P\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}k_{i},-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}\omega_{i}\!\right)\!\prod_{i<j}^{(n)}P(\sigma_{i}k_{i}-\sigma_{j}k_{j},-\sigma_{i}\omega_{i}+\sigma_{j}\omega_{j})\sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}=0 (223)

must hold for n=2,3,…,Nn=2,3,\ldots,N. In (223), PP is the polynomial corresponding to the bilinear operator BB, ∑σ=±1\sum_{\sigma=\pm 1} indicates the summation over all possible combinations of σ1=±1,σ2=±1,…,σn=±1\sigma_{1}=\pm 1,\;\sigma_{2}=\pm 1,\;\ldots,\;\sigma_{n}=\pm 1 and ∏i<j(n)\prod_{i<j}^{(n)} means the product of all possible combinations of the nn elements with i<j,i<j, and all ki,ωik_{i},\omega_{i} subject to the dispersion law ωi​(ki).\omega_{i}(k_{i}). Note that (223) is a condition for PP and not for the kik_{i}. Also, all ωi\omega_{i} are replaced in terms of the kik_{i} because (223) is evaluated on the dispersion law.

For (220), P⁡(Dx,Dt)=B=Dx​Dt+Dx8P(D_{x},D_{t})=B=D_{x}D_{t}+D_{x}^{8} and the three-soliton condition S⁡[P,3]=0S[P,3]=0 (see, (34, Eq. (28))) gives2121 21 Based on symmetry considerations, simplified expressions of (223) are given in (71, Eq. (2.9)) and (83, Eqs. (4.3) and (4.4)). A computer implementation can be found in (126, pp. 27-29 and p. 82).

(k1​k2​k3)4​[(k12−k22)​(k12−k32)​(k22−k32)]2\displaystyle(k_{1}k_{2}k_{3})^{4}\left[(k_{1}^{2}-k_{2}^{2})(k_{1}^{2}-k_{3}^{2})(k_{2}^{2}-k_{3}^{2})\right]^{2}
(k12​k22+k12​k32+k22​k32)​(k14+k24+k34+k12​k22+k12​k32+k22​k32)=0.\displaystyle(k_{1}^{2}k_{2}^{2}+k_{1}^{2}k_{3}^{2}+k_{2}^{2}k_{3}^{2})(k_{1}^{4}+k_{2}^{4}+k_{3}^{4}+k_{1}^{2}k_{2}^{2}+k_{1}^{2}k_{3}^{2}+k_{2}^{2}k_{3}^{2})=0. (224)

Thus, the wave numbers must be either equal, each other’s opposites, or zero. In conclusion, the non-existence of a three-soliton solution agrees with the claim in [51].

8 Soliton Solutions in Multiple Space Dimensions

8.1 The Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation

Arguably, the KP equation [2, 16, 55],

(ut+6​u​ux+u3​x)x+3​σ​uy​y=0(u_{t}+6uu_{x}+u_{3x})_{x}+3\sigma u_{yy}=0 (225)

for u⁡(x,y,t)u(x,y,t) and σ=±1\sigma=\pm 1, is one of the most studied soliton equations involving more than one space variable. We only consider the so-called KPII equation [7, 60] where σ=1\sigma=1. A Laurent series of its solution suggests the transformation u=2​(ln⁡f)x​xu=2\,(\ln f)_{xx}. We therefore integrate (225) twice,

∂t(∫xu​𝑑x)+3​u2+ux​x+3​∂y2(∫x(∫xu​𝑑x)​𝑑x)=0,\partial_{t}\left(\int^{x}u\,dx\right)+3u^{2}+u_{xx}+3\partial_{y}^{2}\left(\int^{x}\left(\int^{x}u\,dx\right)\,dx\right)=0, (226)

before replacing uu in terms of ff. The resulting equation,

f⁡(fx​t+f4​x+3​fy​y)−fx​ft+3​fx​x2−4​fx​f3​x−3​fy2=0,f(f_{xt}+f_{4x}+3f_{yy})-f_{x}f_{t}+3f_{xx}^{2}-4f_{x}f_{3x}-3f_{y}^{2}=0, (227)

can be written in bilinear form

(Dx​Dt+Dx4+3​Dy2)​(f⋅f)=0,\left(D_{x}D_{t}+D_{x}^{4}+3D_{y}^{2}\right)(f\mathbf{\cdot}f)=0, (228)

where DyD_{y} is the Hirota operator defined in a similar way as DxD_{x} and DtD_{t} in (21) and (22), respectively.

Continuing with (227), the computation of soliton solutions is similar to the KdV case in Section 2.2. Indeed, the forms of f⁡(x,y,t)f(x,y,t) for multi-soliton solutions remain the same except that θi=ki​x+li​y−ωi​t+δi\theta_{i}=k_{i}x+l_{i}y-\omega_{i}t+\delta_{i} with ωi=ki4+3​li2ki\omega_{i}=\frac{k_{i}^{4}+3l_{i}^{2}}{k_{i}}. Setting li=ki​Pil_{i}=k_{i}P_{i} simplifies matters. Then θi=ki​(x+Pi​y−(ki2+3​Pi2)​t)+δi\theta_{i}=k_{i}\left(x+P_{i}y-(k_{i}^{2}+3P_{i}^{2})t\right)+\delta_{i} and the phase factors are

ai​j=(ki−kj)2−(Pi−Pj)2(ki+kj)2−(Pi−Pj)2a_{ij}=\frac{(k_{i}-k_{j})^{2}-(P_{i}-P_{j})^{2}}{(k_{i}+k_{j})^{2}-(P_{i}-P_{j})^{2}} (229)

and b123=a12​a13​a23b_{123}=a_{12}\,a_{13}\,a_{23}.

Setting k=2​Kk=2K and δ=2​Δ\delta=2\Delta, we obtain the solitary wave solution

u⁡(x,y,t)=2​K2​sech2​[K⁡(x+P​y−(4​K2+3​P2)​t)+Δ]u(x,y,t)=2K^{2}{\mathrm{sech}}^{2}\left[K\left(x+Py-(4K^{2}+3P^{2})t\right)+\Delta\right] (230)

which is essentially one-dimensional.

The lengthy expressions for the two- and three-soliton solutions are not shown for brevity. A graph of the two-soliton solution of (225) at t=0.35t=0.35 for K1=12,K2=1,P1=−18,P2=316K_{1}=\frac{1}{2},K_{2}=1,P_{1}=-\frac{1}{8},P_{2}=\frac{3}{16} and Δ1=Δ2=0\Delta_{1}=\Delta_{2}=0 is shown in Fig. 21. Various types of soliton interactions have been reported in the literature and observed at flat beaches [1].

8.2 A (3+1)(3+1)-dimensional evolution equation

Consider the (3+1)(3+1)-dimensional evolution equation [21],

3​Wx​z−2​(2​Wt+W3​x−2​W​Wx)y+2​(Wx​∂x−1Wy)x=0,3W_{xz}-2\left(2W_{t}+W_{3x}-2WW_{x}\right)_{y}+2\left(W_{x}\partial_{x}^{-1}W_{y}\right)_{x}=0, (231)

which can be written as

3​ux​x​z−(2​ux​t+u4​x−2​ux​ux​x)y+2​(ux​x​uy)x=03u_{xxz}-\left(2u_{xt}+u_{4x}-2u_{x}u_{xx}\right)_{y}+2(u_{xx}u_{y})_{x}=0 (232)

after substituting W=uxW=u_{x}. Integrating (232) twice with respect to xx, yields

3​uz−2​∂t(∫xuy​𝑑x)−ux​x​y+2​ux​uy=0.3u_{z}-2\partial_{t}\left(\int^{x}u_{y}\,dx\right)-u_{xxy}+2u_{x}u_{y}=0. (233)

A Laurent series solution of (232) suggests the transformation u=−3​(ln⁡f)xu=-3\,(\ln f)_{x} which indeed allows one to replace (233) by a homogeneous equation,

f⁡(−2​fy​t+3​fx​z−fx​x​x​y)+2​fy​ft−3​(fx​fz+fx​x​fx​y−fx​fx​x​y)+f3​x​fy=0,f(-2f_{yt}+3f_{xz}-f_{xxxy})+2f_{y}f_{t}-3(f_{x}f_{z}+f_{xx}f_{xy}-f_{x}f_{xxy})+f_{3x}f_{y}=0, (234)

of the form f​ℒ​f+𝒩⁡(f,f)=0f{\cal L}f+{\cal N}(f,f)=0 with

ℒ​f\displaystyle{\cal L}f =\displaystyle= −2​fy​t+3​fx​z−fx​x​x​y,\displaystyle-2f_{yt}+3f_{xz}-f_{xxxy}, (235)
𝒩⁡(f,g)\displaystyle{\cal N}(f,g) =\displaystyle= 2​fy​gt−3​(fx​gz+fx​x​gx​y−fx​gx​x​y)+f3​x​gy.\displaystyle 2f_{y}g_{t}-3(f_{x}g_{z}+f_{xx}g_{xy}-f_{x}g_{xxy})+f_{3x}g_{y}. (236)

To compute a single solitary wave solution we set f=1+eθf=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}, where θ=k​x+l​y+m​z−ω​t+δ{\theta}=kx+ly+mz-\omega t+\delta. Then, ℒ​eθ=0{\cal L}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta}=0 yields ω=k⁡(k2​l−3​m)2​l\omega=\frac{k(k^{2}l-3m)}{2l}. Since 𝒩⁡(eθ,eθ)=0{\cal N}({\mathrm{e}}^{\theta},{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta})=0 we readily obtain a solitary wave solution

u⁡(x,t)=−32​k​(1+tanh⁡[12​(k​x+l​y+m​z−k⁡(k2​l−3​m)​t2​l+δ)]).u(x,t)=-\frac{3}{2}k\left(1+\tanh\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(kx+ly+mz-\frac{k(k^{2}l-3m)t}{2l}+\delta\right)\right]\right). (237)

For a two-soliton solution we take f=1+eθ1+eθ2+a12​eθ1+θ2,f=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}}+a_{12}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}}, with θi=ki​x+li​y+mi​z−ωi​t+δi\theta_{i}=k_{i}x+l_{i}y+m_{i}z-\omega_{i}t+\delta_{i} and ωi=ki​(ki2​li−3​mi)2​li.\omega_{i}=\frac{k_{i}(k_{i}^{2}l_{i}-3m_{i})}{2l_{i}}. After some computations

a12=k1​k2​l1​l2​(k1−k2)​(l1−l2)−(k1​l2−k2​l1)​(l1​m2−l2​m1)k1​k2​l1​l2​(k1+k2)​(l1+l2)−(k1​l2−k2​l1)​(l1​m2−l2​m1).a_{12}=\frac{k_{1}k_{2}l_{1}l_{2}(k_{1}-k_{2})(l_{1}-l_{2})-(k_{1}l_{2}-k_{2}l_{1})(l_{1}m_{2}-l_{2}m_{1})}{k_{1}k_{2}l_{1}l_{2}(k_{1}+k_{2})(l_{1}+l_{2})-(k_{1}l_{2}-k_{2}l_{1})(l_{1}m_{2}-l_{2}m_{1})}. (238)

Thus, a two-soliton solution exists without having to impose any restrictions on the components (ki,li,mi)(k_{i},l_{i},m_{i}) of the wave vector. In [21], the authors took li=kil_{i}=k_{i} and mi=ki3m_{i}=k_{i}^{3} from the outset and therefore only computed a special two-soliton solution for which ωi=−ki3\omega_{i}=-k_{i}^{3}. Assuming a traveling frame θi=ki​(x+y)+ki3​(t+z)\theta_{i}=k_{i}(x+y)+k_{i}^{3}(t+z) from the start is too restrictive. Indeed, by a change of variables (x,y,z,t)→(ξ,η)(x,y,z,t)\rightarrow(\xi,\eta) with ξ=x+y\xi=x+y and η=t+z\eta=t+z, one can readily show that after two integrations with respect to ξ\xi equation (231) becomes the integrated KdV equation, that is, (17) with tt replaced by η\eta, xx by ξ\xi, and u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) by u⁡(ξ,η)u(\xi,\eta).

Moving on with our computations, a three-soliton solution does not exist for arbitrary wave numbers. Indeed,

f=1+eθ1+eθ2+eθ3+a12​eθ1+θ2+a13​eθ1+θ3+a23​eθ2+θ3+b123​eθ1+θ2+θ3f=1+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}}+{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{3}}+a_{12}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}}+a_{13}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}+\theta_{3}}+a_{23}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{2}+\theta_{3}}+b_{123}{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}+\theta_{3}} (239)

only yields a three-soliton solution if li=kil_{i}=k_{i} with mim_{i} still arbitrary (and a lengthy computation shows that the same holds for a four-soliton solution). The dispersion law and coefficients then simplify into ωi=12​(ki3−3​mi)\omega_{i}=\frac{1}{2}(k_{i}^{3}-3m_{i}), ai​j=((ki−kj)/(ki+kj))2a_{ij}=((k_{i}-k_{j})/(k_{i}+k_{j}))^{2}, and b123=a12​a13​a23b_{123}=a_{12}a_{13}a_{23}, which are the same as for the KdV equation.

9 Symbolic Software

Symbolic software for Hirota’s method comes in two flavors: (i) code that aims at finding the bilinear form of a nonlinear PDE and (ii) code to compute soliton solutions with and without the use of the bilinear form.

9.1 Early developments of soliton software

As part of the design of symbolic software for soliton theory, in the early 1990s Hereman and Zhuang [28, 31, 32, 33] implemented the Hirota method in Macsyma, a commercial computer algebra system now superseded by Maxima2222 22 Maxima is freely available from SourceForge at https://maxima.sourceforge.io/., a descendant of the original DOE Macsyma system. The code HIROTA_SINGLE.MAX is able to automatically compute up to three-soliton solutions of well-known nonlinear PDEs that can be transformed into a single bilinear equation of KdV-type [31, 34], including the KdV, Boussinesq, KP, SK, and shallow water wave equations. To compute soliton solutions of these mostly (1+1)(1+1)-dimensional PDEs, the bilinear form must be given explicitly. The code can also verify condition (223) for the existence of three- or four-soliton solutions (n=3n=3 or 44). To cover bilinear equations of mKdV-type [35], Hereman and Zhuang made HIROTA_SYSTEM.MAX [28, 126] which was applied to various extensions of the mKdV equation taken from [52]. Codes for the sine-Gordon equation, NLS equations, and various other types of soliton equations which have quite complicated bilinear forms [37] were not developed. The code HIROTA_SINGLE.MAX was converted into Mathematica syntax and released under the name hirota.m. Further details about these open source codes2323 23 The codes are still available at https://inside.mines.edu/˜whereman. can be found in [32, 126].

Although the simplified Hirota method (which does not use the bilinear form) was already published in [30, 85], its implementation did not start until 2012 and is still ongoing. Cook et al. [12] developed the Mathematica code Homogenize-And-Solve.m to automate the computation of the soliton solutions discussed in Section 4 and other soliton equations in (1+1)(1+1)-dimensions. That code is now superseded by PDESolitonSolutions.m [22].

9.2 Implementation and Limitations of PDESolitonSolutions.m

The current version of PDESolitonSolutions.m [22] computes up to three-soliton solutions for a given single PDE in one dependent variable (called uu below) which is function of up to three space variables (x,y,z)(x,y,z) and time (t)(t). The PDE must have polynomial terms with constant coefficients. Presently, the code can not handle systems of PDEs. The algorithm largely follows the steps of Section 3.2:

  • (i)

    The PDE is integrated with respect to xx as many times as possible.

  • (ii)

    The code first attempts to find a transformation to homogenize the given PDE based on the (truncated) Laurent series expansion of its solution. If unsuccessful, the code tries a transformation of type u=c​(ln⁡f)n​x,u=c\,(\ln f)_{nx}, with integer 1≤n≤nmax1\leq n\leq n_{\rm max} (with default value nmax=4n_{\rm max}=4) and constant cc. Starting with n=1n=1, the code seeks the lowest value of nn and matching cc so that the PDE is transformed into an equation that is homogeneous in ff.

  • (iii)

    A solution of type f⁡(x,y,z,t)=1+∑n=1pϵn​f(n)​(x,y,z,t)f(x,y,z,t)=1+\sum_{n=1}^{p}\epsilon^{n}\,f^{(n)}(x,y,z,t) is sought where 1≤p≤pmax1\leq p\leq p_{\rm max} (with default value pmax=8p_{\rm max}=8). The bookkeeping parameter ϵ\epsilon helps with splitting expressions into single exponentials, products of two exponentials, etc. Substituting the above sum for ff into a homogeneous equation for ff (of degree dd) yields an expression of degree ℓmax=d​pmax\ell_{\rm max}=d\,p_{\rm max} in ϵ\epsilon.

  • (iv)

    Starting with f(1)=∑i=1Nϕi​(x,y,z,t)f^{(1)}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\phi_{i}(x,y,z,t), where the natural number NN refers to the NN-soliton solution one aims to compute and ϕi​(x,y,z,t)≡eθi\phi_{i}(x,y,z,t)\equiv{\mathrm{e}}^{\theta_{i}} =eki​x+li​y+mi​z−ωi​t+δi={\mathrm{e}}^{k_{i}x+l_{i}y+m_{i}z-\omega_{i}t+\delta_{i}}, at order ϵ\epsilon the code balances the linear terms in ϕi\phi_{i} to determine the dispersion relation ωi​(ki,li,mi)\omega_{i}(k_{i},l_{i},m_{i}).

  • (v)

    Next, based on the monomials in the functions ϕi\phi_{i} that occur at order ϵ2\epsilon^{2}, the code builds f(2)=∑i,jai​j​ϕi​ϕjf^{(2)}=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\phi_{i}\phi_{j} and computes the coefficients ai​ja_{ij} (and possible constraints for ki,li,k_{i},l_{i}, and mim_{i}) by balancing like products of two exponentials. Note that i=ji=j is allowed to account for terms in ϕi2\phi_{i}^{2}.

  • (vi)

    At the next orders in ϵ\epsilon, expressions for f(3),f(4)f^{(3)},f^{(4)}, etc., are computed the same way. If at some order n<pmaxn<p_{\rm max} in ϵ\epsilon the function f(n)f^{(n)} becomes identically zero, the code verifies that f(n+1),…,f(pmax)f^{(n+1)},\ldots,f^{(p_{\rm max})} can be set to zero. It also verifies whether or not the coefficients of ϵn+1,…,ϵℓmax\epsilon^{n+1},\ldots,\epsilon^{\ell_{\rm max}} in the expression mentioned in (iii) all vanish. For non-solitonic equations this may lead to (additional) constraints on the wave numbers. If both verifications are successful, the code returns the solutions after explicitly verifying that the final ff indeed satisfies the homogenized PDE. If none of the f(n)f^{(n)} become zero, the code reports that a NN-soliton solution could not be computed. The code will return a solitary wave solution for N=1N=1 and a bi-soliton solution for N=2N=2, provided such solutions exist.

Some remarks are warranted:

  • (i)

    The current code only considers integration with respect to xx ignoring the possibility to integrate the given PDE with respect to yy or zz.

  • (ii)

    In addition to transformations based on a truncated Laurent series, currently only single-term logarithmic derivative transformations with respect to xx up to fourth-order are used. At present only transformations involving one new dependent variable (f)(f) are considered. Therefore, the current code can not find solutions of, for example, the mKdV equation.

  • (iii)

    With regard to the growing complexity of f(n)f^{(n)} as nn increases, pmax=8p_{\rm max}=8 has been set as default value.

  • (iv)

    The current code is limited to three space variables and time. To prevent long expressions and avoid Mathematica’s conversion of products of exponentials into a single exponential, the explicit form of ϕi​(x,y,z,t)\phi_{i}(x,y,z,t) is never used. Instead, the code uses rules for derivatives of ϕi​(x,y,z,t)\phi_{i}(x,y,z,t), such as ϕi​(x,y,z,t)n​x=kin​ϕi​(x,y,z,t)\phi_{i}(x,y,z,t)_{nx}=k_{i}^{n}\phi_{i}(x,y,z,t) and ϕi​(x,y,z,t)m​t=(−ωi)m​ϕi​(x,y,z,t)\phi_{i}(x,y,z,t)_{mt}=(-\omega_{i})^{m}\phi_{i}(x,y,z,t).

  • (v)

    For example for the two-soliton case, f(2)=a11​ϕ12+a12​ϕ1​ϕ2+a22​ϕ22f^{(2)}=a_{11}\phi_{1}^{2}+a_{12}\phi_{1}\phi_{2}+a_{22}\phi_{2}^{2} where some of these terms might not be included. Indeed, after substitution of f=1+f(1)=1+ϕ1+ϕ2f=1+f^{(1)}=1+\phi_{1}+\phi_{2} into the homogeneous equation, the code generates the list of monomials of type ϕi​ϕj\phi_{i}\phi_{j} (including ϕi2\phi_{i}^{2}) that occur at order ϵ2{\epsilon}^{2} and makes a linear combination of those monomials with undetermined coefficients ai​ja_{ij} to create f(2)f^{(2)} with the minimal number of terms. The coefficients ai​ja_{ij} are then computed by requiring that like terms in ϕi​ϕj\phi_{i}\phi_{j} vanish.

    The same procedure is used to compute NN-soliton solutions. Starting from f=1+f(1)=1+ϕ1+ϕ2+…+ϕNf=1+f^{(1)}=1+\phi_{1}+\phi_{2}+\ldots+\phi_{N}, the code constructs the minimal expressions for all subsequent f(n)f^{(n)} in which each term is a product of nn (not necessarily distinct) functions taken from {ϕ1,ϕ2,…,ϕN}\{\phi_{1},\phi_{2},\ldots,\phi_{N}\}. The code determines which of these products are actually needed and combines them with undetermined coefficients.

  • (vi)

    For homogeneous equations of high degree, some symbolic verifications can be quite slow. To speed things up, the code does no longer symbolically verify that coefficients of higher orders in ϵ\epsilon in the perturbation scheme vanish as soon as two consecutive coefficients of lower orders terms already vanished identically. Once two consecutive expressions are determined to be zero, the code numerically tests if the expressions at higher order are also zero. This applies to both the computation of the f(n)f^{(n)} as well as the coefficients of ϵ\epsilon in the perturbation scheme.

    Furthermore, verifying that the (lengthy) expressions of ff indeed solve the homogeneous equation can be time consuming, especially for cubic and quartic equations. Indeed, checking that (107) satisfies (70) is computationally very expensive. Therefore, after the solution is substituted into the homogeneous equation, all independent variables, wave numbers (ki,li,mi)(k_{i},l_{i},m_{i}), phase constants δi\delta_{i}, and parameters in the PDE (if present) are repeatedly replaced by random real numbers in [−2,2][-2,2]. In each case it is checked if the resulting expression is zero within machine precision. Likewise, the solitary wave and one-soliton solutions for u⁡(x,y,z,t)u(x,y,z,t) are tested symbolically but the numerical approach is used to verify that the often long expressions of two- and three-soliton solutions u⁡(x,y,z,t)u(x,y,z,t) indeed solve the original PDE.

9.3 Other software packages for Hirota’s method

As early as 1988, Ito [53] designed code in REDUCE to interactively investigate nonlinear PDEs with Hirota’s bilinear and Wronskian operators.

In [124], Zhou et al. introduced the Maple package Bilinearization to convert (mainly) nonlinear evolution equations of KdV-type into their bilinear form using logarithmic-derivative transformations. To cover the mKdV and nonlinear Schrödinger equations, they later extended the algorithm to work for arctan\arctan and rational transformations. They also added the code Multisoliton to compute up to three-soliton solutions for single bilinear equations and simple systems of bilinear equations. Ye et al. [120, 121] presented a more efficient method to do the same but only with logarithmic-derivative transformations. Their method is also implemented in Maple. When successful, these Maple codes return the bilinear form explicitly.

Yang and Ruan [117, 118, 119] have produced the Maple packages HBFTrans, HBFTrans2, and HBFGen to transform nonlinear PDEs into their bilinear forms, again based on logarithmic derivative transformations. In their newest algorithms, they take advantage of the properties of the Hirota operators and the scaling invariance2424 24 Dilation or scaling symmetry is a special Lie-point symmetry shared by many integrable PDEs [29]. of the original equation. Doing so, makes their codes more efficient and faster.

Based on the Bell polynomial approach [68, 69], Miao et al. [75] developed the Maple package PDEBellII to compute bilinear forms, bilinear Bäcklund transformations, Lax pairs, and conservation laws of KdV-type equations. In contrast to PDEBell, developed earlier by Yang and Chen, PDEBellII does no longer use scaling invariance to make it applicable to a broader class of nonlinear PDEs.

For completeness, we mention the new computational method of Kumar et al. [62] for the construction of bilinear forms which, as far as we know, has not been implemented yet.

10 Conclusions and Future Work

Hirota’s bilinear method is an effective method to construct soliton solutions of completely integrable nonlinear PDEs. In this paper we discussed a simplified version of Hirota’s method (which does not use Hirota’s bilinear operators) and used it to construct solitary and soliton solutions of various soliton equations as well as some nonlinear polynomial equations that do not have solitons.

We showed that the Hirota transformation is crucial to obtain a PDE that is homogeneous of degree (in the new dependent variable). We focused on logarithmic derivative transformations but, as we saw with the mKdV equation, rational and arctan\arctan transformations might be required, or combinations thereof. To homogenize, e.g., the Davey-Stewartson system, one needs a mixture of rational and logarithmic derivative transformations. There is no systematic way for finding these transformations but the first few terms of a Laurent series solution and scaling invariance of the PDE can help determine a suitable candidate thereby reducing the guess work.

The actual recasting of the transformed PDE into bilinear form in terms of Hirota’s operators, which assumes a quadratic equation or a tricky decoupling into quadratic equations, is not required to compute solitary wave solutions or solitons. Indeed, without bilinear forms, exact solutions of the transformed equation can still be constructed straightforwardly by solving a perturbation-like scheme on the computer using a symbolic manipulation package.

The simplified version of Hirota’s method is largely algorithmic and now available as the Mathematica program PDESolitonSolutions.m. In future releases a broader class of transformations (likely involving two functions ff and gg) will be considered to make the code applicable to a large set of PDEs including mKdV-type equations. A future version of the code might follow the algorithm presented in this paper even closer. It will use the perturbation schemes involving the linear and nonlinear operators which will automatically be generated by splitting the homogeneous equations into linear and nonlinear pieces. This “divide-and-conquer” strategy is expected to make the computations faster. An extension of the algorithm and code to systems of PDEs is being investigated.

For the derivation of the perturbation scheme for equations of type (58) we need Cauchy’s product formula for three sums:

Substituting (28) into (58) and applying (240) and (244) yields the following term in ϵn\epsilon^{n}:

ℒ​f(n)+∑j=1n−1(2​f(j)​ℒ​f(n−j)+𝒩1​(f(j),f(n−j)))+∑j=2n−1∑ℓ=1j−1(f(ℓ)​f(n−j)​ℒ​f(j−ℓ)CLOSE\displaystyle{\cal L}f^{(n)}+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\left(2f^{(j)}{\cal L}f^{(n-j)}+{\cal N}_{1}(f^{(j)},f^{(n-j)})\right)+\sum_{j=2}^{n-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{j-1}\left(f^{(\ell)}f^{(n-j)}{\cal L}f^{(j-\ell)}\right.
OPEN+f(ℓ)​𝒩1​(f(n−j),f(j−ℓ))+𝒩2​(f(ℓ),f(n−j),f(j−ℓ)))=0,n≥3.\displaystyle+\left.f^{(\ell)}{\cal N}_{1}(f^{(n-j)},f^{(j-\ell)})+{\cal N}_{2}(f^{(\ell)},f^{(n-j)},f^{(j-\ell)})\right)=0,\;\;\;n\geq 3. (245)

Quadrilinear scheme

Setting up the perturbation scheme for equations of type (73) requires the formula

(∑p=1∞ϵp​ap)​(∑q=1∞ϵq​bq)​(∑r=1∞ϵr​cr)​(∑s=1∞ϵs​ds)\displaystyle\left(\sum_{p=1}^{\infty}\epsilon^{p}\,a_{p}\right)\left(\sum_{q=1}^{\infty}\epsilon^{q}\,b_{q}\right)\left(\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\epsilon^{r}\,c_{r}\right)\left(\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}\epsilon^{s}\,d_{s}\right)
=∑n=4∞ϵn​∑j=3n−1∑ℓ=2j−1∑m=1ℓ−1am​bn−j​cj−ℓ​dℓ−m.\displaystyle=\sum_{n=4}^{\infty}\epsilon^{n}\sum_{j=3}^{n-1}\sum_{\ell=2}^{j-1}\sum_{m=1}^{\ell-1}a_{m}\,b_{n-j}\,c_{j-\ell}\,d_{\ell-m}. (246)

Substituting (28) into (73) and applying (240), (244), and (246) yields the following at O⁡(ϵn)O(\epsilon^{n}):

ℒ​f(n)+∑j=1n−1(3​f(j)​ℒ​f(n−j)+𝒩1​(f(j),f(n−j)))\displaystyle\!\!{\cal L}f^{(n)}+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\left(3f^{(j)}{\cal L}f^{(n-j)}+{\cal N}_{1}(f^{(j)},f^{(n-j)})\right)
+∑j=2n−1∑ℓ=1j−1(3f(ℓ)f(n−j)ℒf(j−ℓ)+2f(ℓ)𝒩1(f(n−j),f(j−ℓ))+𝒩2(f(ℓ),f(n−j),f(j−ℓ)))\displaystyle\!\!\!+\sum_{j=2}^{n-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{j-1}\left(\!3f^{(\ell)}f^{(n-j)}{\cal L}f^{(j-\ell)}+\!2f^{(\ell)}{\cal N}_{1}(f^{(n-j)},f^{(j-\ell)})+\!{\cal N}_{2}(f^{(\ell)},f^{(n-j)},f^{(j-\ell)})\!\right)
+∑j=3n−1∑ℓ=2j−1∑m=1ℓ−1(f(m)f(n−j)f(j−ℓ)ℒf(ℓ−m)+f(m)f(n−j)𝒩1(f(j−ℓ),f(ℓ−m))\displaystyle\!\!+\sum_{j=3}^{n-1}\sum_{\ell=2}^{j-1}\sum_{m=1}^{\ell-1}\left(f^{(m)}f^{(n-j)}f^{(j-\ell)}{\cal L}f^{(\ell-m)}+f^{(m)}f^{(n-j)}{\cal N}_{1}(f^{(j-\ell)},f^{(\ell-m)})\right.
OPEN+f(m)​𝒩2​(f(n−j),f(j−ℓ),f(ℓ−m))+𝒩3​(f(m),f(n−j),f(j−ℓ),f(ℓ−m)))=0,\displaystyle\left.\!\!+f^{(m)}{\cal N}_{2}(f^{(n-j)},f^{(j-\ell)},f^{(\ell-m)})+{\cal N}_{3}(f^{(m)},f^{(n-j)},f^{(j-\ell)},f^{(\ell-m)})\right)=0,
n≥4.\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\;n\geq 4. (247)

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
